title: Ir, venir, salir
topic: present tense of ir, venir, salir; a, en, de with places; al and del
why: First lesson on irregular verbs in the present: ir, venir and salir let you say where you're going, where you're coming from and when you leave. It also sets up a and de with places, the contractions al and del, and means of transport, which will come back throughout the next unit, in the city.

{"lessons": ["

Voy, vengo, salgo

So far, you've mostly used regular verbs, plus ser, tener and estar. This unit tackles the irregular verbs you need all the time. We start with three verbs of movement: ir (to go), venir (to come) and salir (to go out, to leave).

ir (to go)venir (to come)salir (to go out, to leave)
yovoyvengosalgo
túvasvienessales
él, ella, ustedvavienesale
nosotros, nosotrasvamosvenimossalimos
vosotros, vosotrasvaisveníssalís
ellos, ellas, ustedesvanvienensalen

What to notice

  • Ir looks nothing like its infinitive, a bit like \"to be\" in English: all its forms start with v- and take the endings of an -ar verb (voy, vas, va).
  • Vengo and salgo take a g in the first person, like tengo, which you already know. You'll see this -go family again in the next lesson.
  • Venir works like tener: vienes, viene, vienen with ie, but venimos, venís without ie.
  • Vais has no accent (it's one syllable), whereas venís and salís do.

Vamos means \"we go\", but also \"let's go!\": ¡Vamos! You'll hear it everywhere in Spain.

¿Vienes a la fiesta de Lucía? Sí, voy con Pablo.Are you coming to Lucía's party? Yes, I'm going with Pablo.
", "

Ir a, venir de, salir de: al and del

With a verb of movement, the destination is marked with a (to), and the starting point with de (from). The traps: English says \"go home\" or \"leave the station\" with no preposition, but Spanish always needs one: a destination always takes a.

EnglishSpanish
I'm going to Madrid.Voy a Madrid.
I'm going to Spain.Voy a España.
I'm going to Portugal.Voy a Portugal.
I'm going to the beach.Voy a la playa.
I'm coming from Lyon.Vengo de Lyon.
I'm leaving the station.Salgo de la estación.

Two required contractions

Before the masculine article el, the prepositions a and de merge with it:

  • a + el = al: Voy al cine. (never \"a el cine\")
  • de + el = del: Vengo del trabajo. (never \"de el trabajo\")

These are the only two contractions: a la, a los, a las, de la, de los, de las stay separate. And the pronoun él (with an accent) never contracts: Es el coche de él.

Home, from home

Without an article, casa means \"home\": Voy a casa (I'm going home), Salgo de casa a las ocho (I leave home at eight). Note the prepositions that English leaves out.

To ask about the destination, say ¿Adónde vas? (or ¿A dónde vas?), \"where are you going (to)?\"; for where a trip starts, ¿De dónde vienes? Both have the accent of question words.

Salimos del cine a las diez y vamos a casa.We leave the movie theater at ten and go home.
", "

En tren, en coche, a pie

For means of transport, Spanish uses en where English says \"by\": en bici (by bike), just like en coche (by car). Only one exception to remember: a pie (on foot).

SpanishEnglish
en trenby train
en cocheby car
en autobúsby bus
en metroby subway (metro)
en aviónby plane
en biciby bike
a pieon foot

The everyday word for car in Spain is el coche. In Latin America, you'll mostly hear el carro or el auto.

The meanings of salir

  • to go out of, to leave a place: Salgo del metro en Sol.
  • to go out, to have fun: Los viernes salimos con amigos.
  • to leave, to depart (a train, a bus): El tren sale a las siete y media.

Ir or venir?

Venir means movement toward where the speaker is. When you're moving toward the other person, Spanish usually says ir, where English says \"come\": someone calls you for dinner, and you answer ¡Voy! (I'm coming!).

¿Vienes a cenar? ¡Sí, ya voy!Are you coming to dinner? Yes, I'm coming!
